newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan market turmoil unlikely to batter economy.
newsitem.headline: Japan market turmoil unlikely to batter economy.

text.p: Financial market turmoil which has battered Tokyo share prices and beaten down the yen has raised fears that the real economy may take a hit, but many economists say the risk to growth is still slight.

"That's the $64,000 question...but I think that the stock weakness would have to be sustained for rather longer before it exerts a major impact on sentiment and wealth," said Russell Jones, chief economist at Lehman Brothers Japan.
Tokyo's stock market has been in a determined downslide since late last year, plagued by worries over Japan's economic future, government policies and the financial system's health.
Such concerns have sliced some 10 percent off the Tokyo market's key barometer, the 225-share Nikkei average, since the start of the year and fears of further falls persist.
On Tuesday, the Nikkei closed down 122.18 points at 17,358.16 after bargain-hunting erased some earlier losses.
The yen, meanwhile, has fallen to a nearly four-year low against the dollar as currency market players persist in their belief that the U.S. economy is a far better bet than Japan's.

The greenback touched 118.27 yen in early Tokyo trade on Tuesday, but later languished around 117.80 yen after being first dampened by Japanese jawboning and then bolstered by U.S. reiteration of support for a strong dollar.

Economists agree that in theory the stock market slump could be bad news for an economy still gradually recovering from a prolonged cyclical recession and threatened with a setback due to higher taxes in the fiscal year from April 1.
Weak share prices make it harder for companies to raise capital, either from the market or by borrowing from banks made increasingly cautious by their own battered balance sheets.

"A decline in stock prices could impact the levels of capital investment in Japan," said Andrew Shipley, an economist at brokerage Schroders. "And if stock prices fall, it could negatively impact household sentiment."
The stock price slide thus raises the odds that forecasts of economic growth, which range from under one percent to a bit above two percent for the year from April, may be too bullish.
"The risk on the downside has increased," said Mineko Sasaki-Smith, chief economist at CS First Boston in Tokyo.
Some think that risk is too big to ignore.
The private Fuji Research Institute has calculated that if the Nikkei stays around an average of 17,000 over the next year, growth would be sliced by about 0.5 percent.

"Personal consumption, corporate capital spending and housing investment would be affected," said Fuji Research economist Masaru Takagi, who had forecast 1997/98 growth at about one percent. "(Prime Minister Ryutaro) Hashimoto needs to think about this."
Others, however, argue that the negative effect will be minimal unless share prices fall further and stay lower longer.

"Right now, firms are cash rich and the demand for capital is relatively weak in the real economy," Shipley said. "We haven't reached the point where the decline in stock prices should dramatically affect capital spending."
The household sector also looks relatively immune, since individuals were already made wary of heavy stock investment by the collapse of Japan's 1980s asset-inflation bubble, he added.

Some economists also said the economy was in better shape than 1995, when it managed 0.9 percent growth despite a stock slump which pared the Nikkei to just under 14,400 and a soaring yen which hit 79.75 yen to the dollar in April of that year.
"The impact of the weakness in stocks, which was actually quite prolonged, wasn't that dramatic," Jones said.
Economists agree that the booster effect of a weaker yen on growth is less than it once was because firms have shifted production offshore. A weak yen makes Japanese exports cheaper in dollar terms.
But some say the weaker currency could still help by making exporters more competitive abroad. "The yen's weakness is a major counterbalance, it's good news," Jones said.
If so, why are Japanese officials hinting -- as Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka did again on Tuesday -- that they might intervene to halt the yen's slide?

"There is probably some concern that if it weakens too much, it could snap back in too dramatic a fashion," a foreign economist said. "And it's always the case that they tend to worry about volatility more than absolute levels."
